translationRepairs: He was promoted in succession to grand adviser remonstrating and general who conquers.
He was promoted in succession to grand adviser remonstrating and champion general.
The Chinese title is 冠軍將軍, Champion General; “general who conquers” misreads 冠 as a 征-type campaign verb and is not supported here.
His father Quanru had been provincial chief clerk, general who conquers, and grand master of palace dissemination, and was posthumously made governor of Jing.
His father Quanru had been provincial chief clerk, champion general, and grand master of palace dissemination, and was posthumously made governor of Jing.
Liang Quanru’s offices include 冠軍將軍, Champion General; the original “general who conquers” is the same mistranslation of 冠軍.
At the start of the Xiaochang era he was made general who sweeps bandits, then gradually rose to general of soaring might and palace attendant.
At the start of the Xiaochang era he was made general who sweeps bandits, then gradually rose to general of soaring might and supervising secretary.
The office is 給事中, supervising secretary, not 侍中. Calling it “palace attendant” collapses two distinct posts; the replacement restores the distinction.
He went out as administrator of Luo'an, was then recalled as great general and mobile headquarters bureau director of the ministry of war, and given the added rank of area commander.
He went out as administrator of Luo'an, was then summoned as bureau director of the ministry of war in the Grand General's mobile headquarters, and given the added rank of area commander.
徵拜大將軍行臺兵部郎中 appoints Xin as war-ministry bureau director on the Grand General’s mobile headquarters, not as great general himself.
Out as Administrator of Luo'an commandery; summoned as Great General mobile headquarters bureau director of the Ministry of War, added area commander.
Out as Administrator of Luo'an commandery; summoned as bureau director of the Ministry of War in the Grand General's mobile headquarters, added area commander.

The original does treat 大將軍 as Xin’s own rank, which the Chinese does not support, but the proposed “Ministry of War director” drops 郎中. The corrected literal keeps bureau director under the Grand General’s mobile headquarters.
In the first year of  he was moved to governor of Zhong, his fief was increased by eight hundred households, and he was then transferred to governor of Shao.
In the first year of Baoding he was moved to governor of Zhong, his fief was increased by eight hundred households, and he was then transferred to governor of Shao.
The Chinese dates the move 保定元年; the idiomatic line leaves a blank where the reign name belongs. Restoring Baoding matches the source and the literal.
Xin Qingzhi, courtesy name Qingzhi, came from Dida in Longxi.
Xin Qingzhi, courtesy name Qingzhi, came from Didao in Longxi.
隴西狄道 is Didao in Longxi. “Dida” truncates 道 and is not a recognized form of the county name.
Xin Qingzhi, styled Qingzhi, was a man of Dida in Longxi.
Xin Qingzhi, styled Qingzhi, was a man of Didao in Longxi.
The same native-place 狄道 is truncated to Dida in the literal line; Didao is the required reading.
His father Xianchong had been administrator of Fufeng commandery and was posthumously made inspector of Yong Province.
His father Xianchong had been administrator of Pingyi commandery and was posthumously made inspector of Yong Province.
The commandery is 馮翊, Pingyi, not 扶風 Fufeng. The original substitutes a different Guanzhong commandery.
His father Xianchong was Administrator of Fufeng commandery; posthumously granted Inspector of Yong Province.
His father Xianchong was Administrator of Pingyi commandery; posthumously granted Inspector of Yong Province.
The literal repeats the Fufeng error for 馮翊郡守; Pingyi is the commandery named in the Chinese.
Emperor Xiaoyu ordered Ang to move grain from Tong, Qu, and the other provinces to feed the campaign.
Emperor Gaozu ordered Ang to move grain from Tong, Qu, and the other provinces to feed the campaign.
The issuer is 高祖, the temple name Gaozu of Northern Zhou Emperor Wu. Xiaoyu is not in this sentence and is not a rendering of 高祖.
Emperor Xiaoyu ordered Ang to transport grain conveniently from Tong, Qu, and other provinces to supply them.
Emperor Gaozu ordered Ang to transport grain conveniently from Tong, Qu, and other provinces to supply them.
The literal likewise invents Emperor Xiaoyu for 高祖; Gaozu is the name the Chinese uses.
While Duke of Jin Yuwen Hu ran the government, Ang was shown something like familial favor by Hu; Emperor Xiaoyu deeply resented this.
While Duke of Jin Yuwen Hu ran the government, Ang was shown something like familial favor by Hu; Emperor Gaozu deeply resented this.
高祖以是頗銜之 attributes the resentment to Gaozu, not to an emperor named Xiaoyu.
At the time Duke of Jin Yuwen Hu held power; Ang was somewhat treated as Hu's kin; Emperor Xiaoyu for this bore considerable resentment.
At the time Duke of Jin Yuwen Hu held power; Ang was somewhat treated as Hu's kin; Emperor Gaozu for this bore considerable resentment.
The literal repeats the Xiaoyu misidentification of 高祖 in the same sentence.
When Liang troops besieged Shouchun and Prince of Huai'nan Yuan Yu marched to relieve the city, Zizhi joined Yu's staff in his existing rank.
When Liang troops besieged Shouchun and Prince of Linhuai Yuan Yu marched to relieve the city, Zizhi joined Yu's staff in his existing rank.
臨淮王 is Prince of Linhuai. Prince of Huai'nan would be 淮南王; 淮南 appears only in the next unit as a region, not as Yuan Yu’s title.
At the time Liang forces besieged Shouchun; Prince of Huai'nan Yuan Yu led troops to relieve them; Zizhi in his existing office joined Yu's military staff.
At the time Liang forces besieged Shouchun; Prince of Linhuai Yuan Yu led troops to relieve them; Zizhi in his existing office joined Yu's military staff.
The literal gives Yuan Yu the same false Huai'nan title; 臨淮王 is Prince of Linhuai.
His distant ancestor Qin had been Later Zhao minister of personnel and inspector of Yong; the family settled there and remained.
His great-great-grandfather Qin had been Later Zhao minister of personnel and inspector of Yong; the family settled there and remained.
其高祖欽 uses the kinship grade 高祖, great-great-grandfather, immediately before 父歡. “Distant ancestor” erases that specified generation.
Early in Datong the Han-chi Tuyuhun took up arms in the Southern Mountains, allied with the Longdong Tuyuhun as mutual support.
Early in Datong the Han-chi Tuge took up arms in the Southern Mountains, allied with the Longdong Tuge as mutual support.
漢熾屠各 and 隴東屠各 are Tuge/Chuge groups. Tuyuhun is 吐谷渾, a different people not named in this sentence.
At the beginning of Datong, Han-chi Tuyuhun blocked arms at Southern Mountain, with Longdong Tuyuhun sharing lips and teeth.
At the beginning of Datong, Han-chi Tuge blocked arms at Southern Mountain, with Longdong Tuge sharing lips and teeth.
The literal repeats the Tuyuhun misreading of 屠各; Tuge is the ethnonym in the Chinese.
Before long opening-office Zhao Chang led the armies forward to attack; Gao led commandery troops to combine forces with Chang; thereupon defeated and pacified them.
Before long opening-office Zhao Chang led the armies forward to attack; Gao led commandery troops to combine forces with Chang; thereupon they defeated and pacified them.

The last clause lacks an English subject and should read “they defeated.” Replacing 開府 with unglossed kaifu is unnecessary: this chapter already renders 開府 as opening-office, and that calque is accurate enough here.
Because Du Gao had carried out his mission to the emperor's satisfaction, he was promoted to area commander and made lesser charioteer earl, then sent again to mark out the frontier.

Because Du Gao had carried out his mission to the emperor's satisfaction, he was promoted to area commander and assigned to administer the lesser attendant office, then sent again to mark out the frontier.
治小御伯 is a Northern Zhou court office, not a “lesser charioteer earl.” The proposed “Lesser Attendant (xiaoyubo)” is still awkward; 治 marks administering that lesser attendant office.
Because Gao on embassy accorded with the imperial intent, promoted and granted Area Commander, administered Lesser Chariot Earl, again went to demarcate the border.
Because Gao on embassy accorded with the imperial intent, he was promoted and granted Area Commander, administered the lesser attendant office, and again went to demarcate the border.

The original mistranslates 小御伯 as Lesser Chariot Earl and omits a subject. The office should be the lesser attendant office; the parenthetical xiaoyubo in the proposal is still clumsy in a literal line.
When Gao returned, ordered to lead him up the hall; personally descended from the imperial seat; clasped hands to part.
When Gao was going back, [the Chen emperor] ordered him led up the hall, personally descended from the imperial seat, and clasped hands to part.

及杲還, 執手以別 is Gao’s departure from Chen, with the unnamed host (Chen’s emperor from the preceding units) seeing him off. “When Gao returned” plus a missing subject makes the farewell look like a Zhou-court homecoming.
Emperor Xiaoyu, troubled by the situation, appointed Du Gao proper central upper grand master and sent him to Chen to propose halting the border war and giving the people peace.
Emperor Gaozu, troubled by the situation, appointed Du Gao proper central upper grand master and sent him to Chen to propose halting the border war and giving the people peace.
高祖患之 is Gaozu (Northern Zhou Emperor Wu). Xiaoyu is again an unsupported substitute for the temple name.
At the beginning of Jian'ede of Emperor Wu, he was made chief minister of the city quarter and sent as envoy to Chen.
At the beginning of Jiande of Emperor Wu, he was made chief minister of the city quarter and sent as envoy to Chen.
武帝建德初 is the Jiande era. Jian'ede is a fused transcription error, not a variant of the reign name.
